doc.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Therapy case of a saxophonist
summary: He recounts a saxophone patient freed from guilt about his brother, and how long such change takes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: childhood that for them to be powerful and successful means taking it away from someone else: from a sibling or from a parent that was hurting or a father that was depressed. So they end up feeling they have to hold themselves back. These people operate as though there’s a governor on their motor all the time. They’re able to brilliantly snatch defeat from the jaws of victory. So those people have trouble getting up on the stage and letting themselves play as good as they can. They end up making mistakes, self-sabotage. In the course of psychotherapy they may be able to understand this theme and re-work it and get freed up and I’ve certainly had patients who were performers who have done just that. I mean one saxophone player I recall years ago who seemed to be getting criticized by the members of his band all the time because he wasn’t playing well enough, but he brought tapes in for me to hear, and I could hear that he had tremendous talent. And in the course of our work it emerged that he felt very guilty that he was favored over his younger brother as he was growing up. Because of that guilt he felt he didn’t have a right to be better than the other members of his band. It was as if he had siblings in his band, and he couldn’t repeat this crime again. So he leveled himself, even put himself lower than his bandmates, even though he really was the best player in the band. And gradually over the course of psychotherapy he felt freed up from that belief and began to really unfurl musically, and he was out there on the bandstand kicking ass.
Wow. That is very interesting. And how long would something like that take? It doesn’t happen overnight for a person.

No it doesn’t. It depends on how firmly entrenched the underlying belief is. And how traumatic the situations were when that belief was created in childhood, so that there’s a spectrum. But you’re right, it doesn’t happen overnight. Sometimes you get quite a bit of change in a matter of months, sometimes it takes years.

Wow. It seems to me you have to — especially classical people — you have to redefine what a mistake is if they’re going to try to improvise. Mistakes — the definition of a mistake changes a lot from classical music to improvised music. But sometimes that’s hard to — it’s easy to say.
